outline.chapter_title: I. Case Background and Procedural History
outline.description: This chapter sets the factual and procedural context of United States v. Constantinescu, explaining who the defendants are, how the indictment alleges a pump‑and‑dump scheme, and the district court’s dismissal and the appeal to the Fifth Circuit.
subtopics: Profiles of the defendants and their social‑media presence
Summary of the charge allegations (conspiracy and securities‑fraud counts)
District court dismissal reasoning (failure to state an offense)
Appeal and court’s mandate to review sufficiency de novo

outline.chapter_title: II. Sufficiency of Indictments: Legal Standards and Prior Fifth Circuit Guidance
outline.description: This chapter explains the Fifth Circuit’s framework for reviewing indictments, drawing from controlling authority and key case law, and outlines the material elements that must be alleged in a securities‑fraud indictment.
subtopics: De novo review requirement per United States v. Rafoi
Four desiderata for a sufficient indictment (enumeration, notice, double‑jeopardy protection)
Application to securities fraud – prasmatism of mail and wire‑fraud analogies
Case law: United States v. Fontenot, Gaytan, Guzman‑Ocampo

outline.chapter_title: III. The Statutory Framework for Securities Fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1348 & § 1349)
outline.description: This chapter analyzes the language of the statutes, the court’s interpretative approach, and how the statute traditionally draws from mail and wire‑fraud doctrines. It then distills the two essential elements—scheme to defraud and intent to defraud—required by § 1348.
subtopics: Statutory purpose and scope of § 1348 and § 1349
Mail and wire‑fraud analogies in securities‑fraud analysis
Scheme‑to‑defraud element: material misrepresentation and deception
Intent‑to‑defraud element: focusing on deceit and harm
Supreme Court guidance: Ciminelli, Kousisis, and recent dicta

outline.chapter_title: IV. Application of Fraud Theories: Right‑to‑Control vs. Fraudulent‑Inducement
outline.description: This chapter contrasts the rejected right‑to‑control theory applied in Ciminelli with the fraudulent‑inducement theory employed in the present case, explaining why the indictment squarely falls under the latter and protects money and property interests.
subtopics: Ciminelli’s right‑to‑control theory and its dismissal
Defendants’ alleged right‑to‑control theory in the indictment?
Fraudulent‑inducement theory (material misstatement to induce a contract for money/property)
Why the indictment does not invoke right‑to‑control theory
Supreme Court endorsement of fraudulent‑inducement in Kousisis
Linking the indictment’s allegations of inducement to a protected property interest

outline.chapter_title: V. Alleged Intent to Defraud: Profit Motive vs. Economic Loss
outline.description: This chapter examines the defendants’ argument that intent to defraud requires a victim’s loss, the Court’s holding in Kousisis that such a requirement is not necessary, and how the indictment’s language about profit and deception satisfies the intent element.
subtopics: Defendants’ claim that profit motive is insufficient
Kousisis decision on the requirement of economic loss
Indictment’s allegations of posting false information to induce purchases
Analysis of “obtain money or property” obligation of the statute
How dismissal of the right‑to‑control theory does not preclude fraudulent‑inducement
Conclusion that intent to defraud is adequately alleged

outline.chapter_title: VI. Holding, Outcome, and Practical Implications
outline.description: This chapter summarizes the court’s holding, explains remand logistics, and discusses the broader impact on prosecutions of social‑media influencers and on the application of securities‑fraud statutes.
subtopics: Reversal of district court dismissal and remand directive
Remand procedural considerations (retrial, further pleading, etc.)
Implication for future securities‑fraud indictments involving social‑media influencers
Potential effect on the scope of the fraudulent‑inducement theory
Key take‑aways for law students concerning indictment sufficiency and fraud theory application
